Hey, it's Evan at OpenAI. I spent my whole career in news, and now I'm here to help journalists use AI to work smarter and faster. So we've all typed a prompt, gotten a weird answer, and thought, "Well, that was useless." We're here to tell you it is not you, it's your prompts, but we can help. Let's start with, what is a prompt? Honestly, it's just instructions. Clear, thorough, well-structured instructions. Good prompting is mostly giving clear directions. For journalists, the trick is to brief ChatGPT the way you would brief a smart newsroom colleague who just walked into the room and has no idea what you're about to say. Think of it this way. A good prompt answers six simple questions. What role should ChatGPT take? What do you want it to do? What background does it need? What should the answer look like? What should it avoid? And what should it double-check before it answers? That is role, task, context, output, limits, and check. Basically, the newsroom version of giving a clear assignment. Let me show you an example. I open up my ChatGPT window and attach a document and write, "Summarize this." Okay. Points for brevity, but this prompt is not good. It is essentially the AI version of walking into a restaurant and saying, "I will have the food." So let's give it a real job. Here's the prompt. "You are helping a local news reporter. Read this city council agenda item. Give me the main points in plain English, any money involved, who's affected, what changed, three questions to ask officials, and one sentence I could say to a viewer. If something is missing, tell me what is missing. Do not guess." Now the AI knows what it's supposed to do. It is not just summarizing, it is helping you get ready to report. First, the role. We told ChatGPT it's helping a local news reporter. That one sentence changes the whole target. Second, task. We told it what to read and what to pull out. Third, context. We said what kind of document this is and who the explanation is for. Fourth, output. We asked for money, affected people, changes, questions, and a viewer takeaway. Fifth, limits. We said, "Do not guess." This is an excellent rule for AI and quite frankly, for humans. And sixth, we asked what is missing. That is the tiny phrase that can save you from a very confident wrong answer. This is why prompting is really a journalism skill. You're not just trying to get nicer words, you're trying to get a cleaner next step. And for journalists in particular, here are two more things to think about. First, a good prompt should send you back to the evidence. Documents, named individuals, missing facts, and claims that need a phone call. Second, if it might touch reporting, ask for uncertainty, missing information, and questions to take to real people. You can do that, and it works. Follow OpenAI Academy for more tips.
